name: Black seed oil hair
lead: Black seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Nigella sativa, also called black cumin. Its best-known constituent is thymoquinone [1][2]. It is promoted in some communities for hair thickness and loss, often applied to the scalp or taken orally.

The sources reviewed contain no hair studies of black seed oil. Published research on it concerns other conditions, and Wikipedia notes insufficient high-quality clinical evidence that the seeds or oil treat human diseases [1].
infobox: Folk medicine in Africa and Asia

paras: Seeds have been found at ancient Egyptian sites, including Tutankhamun's tomb, and Avicenna's Canon of Medicine describes their medicinal use [1]. A 2008 review discusses the therapeutic potential of black cumin [2].

No studies found for hair. Registered human trials of black seed oil examine other conditions, such as osteoarthritis [3], asthma [4], type 2 diabetes [5] and hypertension [6]. Laboratory research on thymoquinone has focused largely on cancer cells [7].

card.summary: Nigella sativa oil promoted for hair, with research on it centred on other conditions and none found on hair.
card.aka: Nigella sativa oil, black cumin oil, kalonji oil

quick.overview:
Black seed oil comes from Nigella sativa seeds and has a long folk-medicine history. Some people use it for hair growth or thickness.

The sources reviewed contain no hair studies; the research on it covers other conditions and laboratory work on thymoquinone.
quick.mechanism: Its main active compound is thymoquinone, studied mostly for anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in the lab. A hair mechanism was not established in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: The FDA classifies the plant as generally recognized as safe as a spice or flavoring; this concerns food use, and the sources reviewed did not cover safety of the oil on the scalp.
